ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
NPAs of State Finance Corporation 
*201. DR. ABRAR AHMED: 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of State Finance Corporations are 
very sick and burdened with a large amount of Non-Performing Assets; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) in what manner Government proposes to rehabilitate the State Finance 
Corporations and deal with their large Non-Performing Assets? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH); (a) to (c) A Statement is placed on the Table -f the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Out of the 18 State Finance Corporations (SFCs) four, that is of, Delhi, 
Kerala, Rajasthan and West Bengal have a positive net worth as on 31 st March. 
2002. The net worth, however, of the remaining 14 SFCs stands fully eroded. 
The accumulated losses of all these SFCs, during 2001-02, aggregates to Rs. 
4,198 crores. NPAs of SFCs as a whole were 61% of the loans and advances, 
as at the end of Marcn 2002.1 he amount involved is Rs. 7076 crores. 
Standard Assets constitute only 39%. 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2002] 
(c) The SFCs Act was amended in 2000 for providing flexibility and 
functional autonomy to them. A Committee headed by Shri G.P. Gupta, the 
then CMD, IDBI looked into their functioning and submitted a report 
recommending, inter-alia, financial, operational and organisational re-
structuring of SFCs. The report of th e Committee has been sent to various 
SFCs for taking immediate action on recommendations that do not involve any 
financial support, such as operational a nd organisational restructuring. SFCs 
being State entities, the State Governme nts are the principal stakeholders. 
They are thus expected to consider steps for improving the performance and 
recapitalisation of SFCs. In order to attract long term refinance from Financial 
Institutions, SFCs have to improve recovery of NPAs and reestablish their 
viability.

Exploration of oil and natural gas in Krishna-Godawari basin 
*202. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of PETRO-
LEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the present status of exploration of oil and natural gas in 
Krishna-Godawari basin in Andhra Pradesh by ONGC; 
(b) whether any headway has been achieved in finding oil and gas reserves 
in the basin; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS {SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Besides acquiring 32,574 Ground Line Kms. (GLK) of 2D and 
19,799 GLK of 3D of seismic data, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. 
(ONGC) has drilled 323 exploratory and 27 development wells in Krishna-
Godavari (KG) onland basin in the State of Andhra Pradesh as on 
01.10.2002.These exploratory efforts of ONGC in Andhra Pradesh have led to 
the discovery of 41 hydrocarbon finds, of which 8 are oil and gas finds and 33

SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, my good friend and the hon. Member 
has drawn into the ambit of his question, a number of adventurous economic 
points, and I would endeavour to respond to each one of them. 
Firstly, I would say that his choice of the adjective that the interest rates 
have 'collapsed' is a disputable adj ective. We, of course, in the Finance 
Ministry, do not agree to the word 'colla pse'.This is a deliberate decision that 
has been taken progressively. The interest rate management is a function of 
the Central Bank, which is the Reserve Bank of India, and, certainly, in 
today's circumstances, for the hon. Member to suggest that there is any 
collapse of any kind in interest rates,  thereby suggesting that there is a 
deflationary situation, etc., when, in fact, manufacturing index Is going up, is 
very adventurous economic thinking. 
With regard to the second aspect of his question where he suggests that we 
have, in any sense, been persuaded by the interest rates management or the 
Reserve Bank of India has been persuaded by the management, in any form 
of competetion, with developed countries, I would say that no, we are not in 
competition with them. The Reserve Bank of India manages the interest rates 
entirely In accordance with the country's fiscal and monetary requirements. 
The third thing that he wishes to know is, will we be able to move back—
particularly, for the deposit interest rates—from say, roughly, 6 per cent to 13 
per cent? Frankly speaking. Madam, I do not see how, in the near future,-we 
can go back to a deposit rate system of 13 per cent. But, as I said just to a 
question earlier, that we, the Government, is fully alive to the difficulties that 
have been caused, in consequence, by a decline in the deposit rates, and we 
are addressing this question so that th e investor is somehow compensated for 
this.

Linking of Mahanadi with southern rivers 
*217. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Peninsular Grid linking Orissa's Mahanadi with major south 
ern rivers was found technically feasible in a study by National Water 
Development Agency; 
(b) whether this project if implemented, could go a long way in solving 
water scarcity problems of States of  Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra 
Pradesh; 
(c) whether this would save water of Mahanadi going waste and flowing 
into the sea; and 
(d) whether Government propose to take up this project, if so, by when? 
38 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES {SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI) : (a) to (d) tn 1980, the Ministry of Water Resources, then known as 
the Ministry of Irrigation, formulated a National Perspective Plan for 
integrated water resources development through inter-linkages of several 
southern-based Peninsular rivers and the Himalayan rivers. The Government 
of India established the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) in 
1982 as an autonomous society to ca rryout water balance and feasibility 
studies of the Peninsular and Himalayan rivers. The -Peninsular Component 
of the National Perspective Plan envisages inter-llnking of Mahanadi-
Godavari-Krishna-Pennar-Cauvery-Vaigai. As per the water balance studies 
of various river basins of the penins ular Component conducted by National 
Water Development Agency, Mahanadi and Godavari river basins are surplus 
in water, whereas the river basins namely. Krishna, Pennar, Cauvery and 
Vaigai are deficit. It is. therefore, pr oposed to transfer the surplus water of 
Mahanadi which in turn will be receiving water from the Himalayan 
component and Godavari basins to Krishna basin by inter-linking Mahanadi 
to Godavari and Godavari to Krishna.  The water, thus received in Krishna 
basin is proposed to be transferred to Pennar, Cauvery and Vaigai basins. 
NWDA has identified 9 links under this part of the Peninsular Component for 
preparation of feasibility report and has prepared f easibility reports for three 
links. Implementation of the water transfer links would only be possible if the 
concerned co-basin States agree to the water linkage proposal and provide 
other logistical support necessary for project implementation and availability 
of fund is ensured.

companies, which came out with public  issues, have been identified as 
'vanishing companies'.

Commission of the State.

the States and suggest a plan by wh ich the Governments, collectively and 
severally, may bring about a restructuring of the public finances restoring

financing of Disaster Management wi th reference to the National Calam 
ity Contingency Fund and the Calami ty Relief Fund and make appropri

(RBI) contain several structural meas ures to improve the efficiency of 
financial system apart from monetary policy measures and signals for soft 
interest rate regime.

transparency in the conduct of monetary policy and provide information to

assessment of overall macro-economic situation. Initiatives of RBI towards a

Features of the Special VRS for the employees declared surplus 
(a) All permanent employees rendered surplus irrespective of their age and 
qualifying service can opt for the scheme. 
(b) An optee of Special VRS will be entitled to receive an ex-gratia 
amount equal to basic pay plus dearness allowance for the number of days 
worked out on the basis of length of service @ 35 days for each completed 
year and 25 days for each remaining year. For any part of a year, the number of 
days, for ex-gratia-amount, will be worked out on the basis of 365 days in a 
year. The ex-gratia amount will be further subject to the following conditions : 
(i)    Total number of years to be counted for payment of ex-gratia will 
not exceed 33 years; 
(ii)    No weightage of additional service will be given for the purpose 
of calculation of ex-gratia; 
(iii) The ex-gratia will be subject to a minimum of Rs. 25,000/- or 250 
days emoluments, whichever is higher; 
(iv) The ex-gratia amount should not exceed the sum of the basic pay 
plus DA that the employee would draw at the prevailing level for 
the balance of the period of service left before superannuation; 
(v)    The ex-gratia amount will be paid in lump sum; 
(vi) The ex-gratia amount up to Rs. 5.00 lakhs will be exempted from 
Income Tax;

given under CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972 to such permanent surplus 
employees who have rendered a minimum of 15 years of qualifying

Guidelines for foreign Banks 
1421. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are any guidelines i ssued by the Reserve Bank of India 
to regulate the functioning of foreign Banks in India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the RBI exercises any effective control on these foreign Banks 
and if so, in what manner; 
(d) whether the foreign banks are permitted to close down their business in 
India at any time without due notice to concerned authorities; and 
(e) if so, the steps taken by the RBI in such cases to safeguard the 
96 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
deposits of the public? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (c) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is empowered under the Banking Regulation 
Act, 1949 to regulate functioning of all the banks in India, including foreign 
banks. All guidelines issued by RBI for regulating the functioning of banks in 
India are equally applicable to foreign banks. RBI's control over the foreign 
banks is the same as over domestic banks. 
(d) and (e) No, Sir.The foreign banks are required to give prior notice, to 
RBI, of their intention to close down their operations in India.The bank 
intending to close down its operation in India is required to discharge all its 
liabilities, realise assets and clear all obligations under contingent liabilities, 
before it is permitted by RBI to close operations in India. RBI ensures that 
foreign bank closes its operation in India only after meeting all liabilities in 
India including liabilities to depositors and investors.

Report on safe drinking water 
1504. SHRI CR THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken note of the report published by Third 
World Academy of Science on 'Safe Drinking Water'; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c)whether it is a fact that India has to face severe water scarcity as per the 
report; and 
(d) if so, the action proposed by Government to deal with the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The report published by Third World Academy of Science on "Safe 
Drinking Water" states that the majority of the world's population does not 
have access to safe drinking water. This is certainly true in most parts of 
Africa and Asia. Even in relatively adva nced countries such as India, safe 
drinking water is not readily available, particularly in rural areas. Together 
these sources account for just 1 per cen t of all water on earth. Six billion 
people depend on freshwater supply (available from rivers, lakes, 
underground sources and aquifers) and a significant portion of the world's 
population now face water shortages. Today 31 countries representing 2.8 
billion people, including China, India, Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria and Peru, 
confront chronic water problems. Total withdrawals of freshwater have 
increased dramatically in 
165 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2002] 
recent times. The groundwater aquifers are currently being depleted faster 
than they are being replenished in parts of India, China and the United States. 
The report narrates some success stories of augmenting supply of water and 
water harvesting and community farming in Rajasthan achieved by Tarun 
Bharat Sangh. The report also speaks about ways to save and replenish water, 
making water safe and potable, making waste water fit for use again and 
technology to make safe drinking water. 
(c) The average annual water availability in the river-systems of the 
country is assessed at 1869 Billion C ubic Metre (BCM). According to the 
International Criteria, a situation of annual water availability of less than 1000 
cubic metre per capita is considered as scarcity condition. The per capita 
water availability in India is 1820 cubic metre per year (2001). However, due 
to spatial variability of rain in the co untry and also because of variation in 
population density, per capita average annual availability of water in different 
basins presently varies from 16,990 cubic metre in Minor River Basins draining 
into Bangladesh & Myanmar, 13,636 cubic metre in Brahmaputra-Barak basin 
to 298 cubic metre in Sabarmati basin. Presently, per capita water availability 
in some river basins namely. Area of  Inland Drainage in Rajasthan Desert; 
Sabarmati; East Flowing Rivers between Mahanadi and Kanyakumari; Pennar; 
West Flowing Rivers of Kutchh, Saurashtra including Luni; Cauvery; Tapi and 
Mahi is in scarcity cdondition. Further, temporal variability in rainfall also 
creates temporary scarcity of water in certain years. In year 2025, the per 
capita water availability has been estimated as 1341 cubic metre per year on a 
national level. The river basins Krishna, Subarnarekha and Ganga are also 
likely to come under the category ot scarce basins. 
(d) To address the problem of water scarcity in the country, emphasis is 
being made to augmei*:t storages through constructioa of dams, speedy 
completion of ongoing water resources projects, other means for water 
harvesting and conservation, and non-conventionaJ measures like interlinking 
of rivers. The National Perspective Plan for water resources development 
envisages interlinking between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers 
for transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit basins to provide 
benefits of drinking water supply, irrigation, hydro-power, flood control, 
navigation, fisheries, salinity and pollution control etc.

Distress sale of Paddy by farmers In Andhra Pradesh 
DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam Deputy 
Chairman, this year, my home State, Andhra Pradesh, has experienced the 
w/orst drought. As reported, the rainfall was 34 per cent less than the normal 
rainfall. Despite this, the paddy grower s have grown their crop in whatever 
way they can. Normally, 7 million tonnes of paddy is grown in the State, but 
it is estimated that this year, the paddy yield is around 48 lakh tonnes only, 
which has affected the farmers very ba dly. But the miseries of the hapless 
farmers are far from over, as the paddy is lying unsold with them. There are 
no takers for the paddy in the State. The Food Corporation of India is not 
purchasing the paddy under one pretext or the other. The rice mill owners too 
are reluctant to purchase the paddy, l eaving the farmers high and dry. Thus, 
practically, the MSP declared for paddy has become redundan t in the State. 
The paddy farmers have started distress sale of their produce, resulting in a 
great loss to the farmers of the State. 
1, therefore, earnestly appeal to the Central Government to come to 
the rescue of the poor paddy growers of Andhra Pradesh and direct the FCI 
and other Government agencies to purchase the entire paddy stock of the 
farmers at the MSP declared by the Go vernment, without further loss of time, 
and save the paddy farmers of Andhra Pradesh who might resort to 
194 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the extreme step of committing suicide, if the situation is not checked in time.   
Thank you. Sir. 
Demand for upgrading Sambalpur University to Central University 
MS. PRAMII-A BOHIDAR (Orissa):  Madam Deputy Chairperson, 
the Sambalpur University serves as the chief educational centre for the entire 
western parts of Orissa. The Sambalpur University was established on is'" 
January, 1967. It is  the second biggest affiliating University in the State of 
Orissa, with jurisdiction exceeding over ten districts of the western parts of 
Orissa. They are Sambalpur, Sundergarh, Bargarh, Jharsuguda, Bolangir, 
Deogarh, Soudh, Suvernapur, Kalahandi, Nuapara and Athamallik subdivision 
of Angul. 
The entire area under the jurisdicti on of this University in Western 
Onssa is both economically and educa tionally backward. The Government of 
India has launched the KBK Programme  in these districts to eradicate 
backwardness. The Scheduled Castes an d the Scheduled Tribes constitute 46 
per cent of the total population of this region, against the Orissa State average 
of 38 per cent and the nati onal average of 22 per cent. The Scheduled Castes, 
the Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes constitute more than 90 
per cent of the total population in this region. Out of a total of 87 very 
backward blocks in Orissa, 67 blocks are located in Western Orissa. 
In the absence of adequate fund, the State Government, in spite of 
its eagerness and willingness to help the University, is unable to do so. 
Unless the Central Government comes to its aid, this University, created to 
serve a backward region of the country,' is sure to suffer stagnation and 
become irrelevant to the socio-economic grovirth of the region. 
Orissa does not have any Central University, at present. In view of 
the above-mentioned facts, the Central Government should consider our 
demand for upgrading Sambalpur University to a Central University. Thank 
you.

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Na du): Sir. the Unit Trust of 
India is a statutory corporation, established under the Unit Trust of India Act,

High dividends, sale and repurchase price of units, unrelated to the 
actual earnings, and other shortcomings in the UTI's working led to a fall in 
the Net Asset Value of the units. These inherent weaknesses, coupled with the 
problems of the capital market in March, 2001, resulted In the US-64 Scheme 
facing a substantial redemption during the months of April-May, 2001, 
forcing temporary suspension of the sale and repurchase under the US-64 
Schemefor a period of six months, that is. up to   31^' December, 2001. 
Depressed capital market and the serious move to restrict the 
Government's liability resulted in the bifurcation of the UTI into two parts, 
namely, Unit-I, comprising the guaranteed portion, and Unit-ll, comprising all 
Net Asset Value-based Schemes, and. in the repeal of the UTI Act, 1963. This 
division provides for and facilitates bifurcation of assets and liabilities of the 
UTI into two parts, that is, specified undertakings and specified companies, 
thereby distancing the Central Government from the UTI and Mutual Fund 
activities.
